summaries.example: Imagine a coach choosing between two fair ways to help a team. One choice may lead to a better result, but the coach might still make the best choice possible after thinking carefully. Philosophers ask whether a perfectly good being must always choose the very best result, or whether choosing wisely and caring about others is enough.
summaries.summary: This entry explores what philosophers mean by perfect goodness, especially when they discuss God as an absolutely perfect being. Perfect goodness may mean perfection overall, but the main focus is moral goodness: having excellent desires and character and acting in an unsurpassably good way. The discussion asks whether this goodness is really possible, whether it exists in an absolutely perfect being, and whether it must belong to that being in every possible situation. Difficult questions arise about evil, freedom, moral rules, and reason. One important debate concerns worlds: if there is always a better world that could have been made, does no choice count as perfectly good? Another asks whether moral goodness is a perfection that every kind of perfect being must have, or whether it depends partly on the kind of being involved.
key_ideas: The phrase “perfect goodness” can mean being perfect in every way, or it can mean one special kind of perfection: moral goodness.
Philosophers often connect perfect goodness with caring about the well-being of people and other beings that can feel.
Some ask whether a perfectly good being must be good in every possible situation, or only in the situation that actually occurs.
A world can contain bad things even if someone believes a perfectly good and powerful being exists. Philosophers disagree about what this shows.
There is a puzzle about freedom: can someone be truly free and morally responsible if doing wrong is never a real possibility?
The entry also asks whether human moral rules apply to an absolutely perfect being in exactly the same way.
summaries.why_it_matters: These questions help us examine what “good” means and whether goodness depends on actions, intentions, results, or character. They also show why simple answers about perfection can lead to deeper questions about choice, responsibility, suffering, and fairness. Thinking carefully about these issues can make our own moral discussions more thoughtful, even when people disagree.

important_terms.definition: The idea that a being has goodness, wisdom, power, and other excellent qualities as fully as possible.
Being as good as possible in desires, character, and actions, especially in how one treats living and feeling beings.
A rule or standard about what someone ought to do.
The ability to make choices and act without being forced by something outside oneself.
A complete way things could be, including what exists and what happens.

questions_to_think_about: Must the best person always produce the best possible result?
Can a choice be good even when every available choice has some drawback?
Is someone free if they never want to do what is wrong?
Should the same moral rules apply to every kind of thinking being?

summaries.example: Suppose an agent must choose one world to bring about, but every available world has another possible world that would contain more value. If moral goodness simply means producing the best state of affairs, then no choice could be morally unsurpassable. But if actions are judged partly by how an agent deliberates, the agent may have reasons not to compare worlds endlessly—especially if doing so would prevent any decision. The debate turns on whether the value of outcomes exhausts the reasons relevant to action.
summaries.summary: The entry investigates perfect goodness within the framework of perfect being theology, while noting that goodness could also be studied without that theological framework. Its central subject is perfect goodness as a specific excellence of agency: the best possible desires, character, and actions, usually understood in familiar welfare-oriented moral terms. Several distinctions organize the discussion. Perfect goodness might be necessary to an absolutely perfect being or merely contingent. It might be actually exemplified, merely possible, or impossible. And moral goodness might be a pure perfection—good for any perfect being—or an impure perfection whose standards depend on the kind of agent involved. The argument from evil raises doubts about actual exemplification, but the entry focuses more specifically on whether perfect goodness is coherent and possible. A major challenge comes from no-best-world cases: if every world an agent could create has a better alternative, perhaps no act of creation is morally unsurpassable. Replies distinguish the value of states of affairs from the quality of deliberative action and appeal to second-order or exclusionary reasons. Further tensions concern whether moral norms can apply to a being unable to violate them, whether necessary goodness is compatible with freedom, and whether perfect freedom and rationality can coexist with necessary moral goodness. The entry presents these as unresolved philosophical disputes rather than as settled conclusions.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes perfect goodness as perfection in general from perfect goodness as a specific practical and usually moral excellence of agency.

It is controversial whether an absolutely perfect being is necessarily morally perfect or is morally perfect only contingently. Necessity might itself be a perfection, but necessary perfect goodness may be incoherent.
The existence of evil is one challenge to the actual exemplification of perfect goodness, although the entry does not attempt to settle the broader problem of evil.

A “no best world” argument claims that if every world has a morally better alternative, then no act of choosing a world is unsurpassable. Critics distinguish evaluating a world from evaluating the agent’s deliberation and action.

Necessary moral goodness appears to conflict with some accounts of freedom, especially those requiring a genuine ability to do otherwise. Other accounts allow free action even when wrongdoing is not a serious possibility.
Whether moral goodness is a pure perfection remains open. Some moral theories focus on human conditions, while others ground morality in value or reasons that might apply to all rational beings.
summaries.why_it_matters: The analysis tests broad claims about God, morality, and perfection by separating issues that are often run together: outcomes and agency, necessity and contingency, freedom and responsibility, and human norms and divine norms. It also warns against assuming that a feature perfect for one kind of thing must belong to an absolutely perfect being. These distinctions matter for debates about the problem of evil, arguments for God’s existence, moral realism, and the nature of practical reason.

important_terms.definition: An approach in philosophical theology that explains God by asking what features an absolutely perfect being would have.
A particular excellence of agency involving desires, character traits, and actions that are morally unsurpassable.
A feature that is good to have without depending on belonging to a limited kind, such as a particular species.
A feature that counts as excellent for a certain kind of thing but depends on that kind’s limitations or nature.
A claim about what could or could not be the case, including whether a property belongs to a being necessarily or only contingently.
The view that freedom requires the possibility of choosing otherwise in a relevant situation.
A reason to refrain from treating another, first-order reason as relevant to one’s deliberation.
The view that moral requirements are closely connected to, or are themselves, requirements of rationality.

questions_to_think_about: Does a better outcome always make the action producing it morally better?
Can an action be unsurpassable even when its outcome is not the best possible outcome?
Is the ability to do otherwise necessary for moral responsibility?
If a perfectly rational agent has decisive moral reasons, does acting morally remain free?
What would show that moral goodness is a pure rather than an impure perfection?

summaries.example: A student council must choose a community project. Project A helps many people, while Project B helps slightly fewer people but can be completed safely and fairly. There may be no project that is best in every respect. One question is whether the council’s decision should be judged only by the project’s result or also by whether the members considered the relevant reasons responsibly. Philosophers use similar questions when discussing whether a perfectly good being could choose a world when no single world is best.
summaries.summary: This entry asks what perfect goodness means and whether it can belong to an absolutely perfect being. The phrase can refer to perfection in general, but the main discussion treats it as a special excellence of agency: having the best possible desires and character and acting in the best possible way. This is normally understood as moral goodness, including concern for human and other sentient well-being. The entry considers whether such goodness is actually exemplified, whether it is even possible, and whether it must be possessed necessarily rather than only contingently. One challenge involves a no-best-world scenario. If every world an agent could bring about has a better alternative, then perhaps no choice could be perfectly good. Some philosophers resist this by saying that an action is not judged in exactly the same way as the state of affairs it produces. The entry also examines whether moral rules can apply to a being that cannot break them, whether necessary goodness leaves room for freedom, and whether freedom and rationality can fit together with perfect goodness. Finally, it asks whether moral goodness is a pure perfection or a quality that depends on the kind of being involved. The source presents competing positions and leaves several questions open.
key_ideas: Philosophers separate being perfect overall from having one particular perfection, such as moral goodness.
Perfect moral goodness is usually described through excellent agency: good motives, character, and actions, including concern for the welfare of sentient beings.
A debate asks whether perfect goodness must belong to an absolutely perfect being by necessity or only in the actual circumstances.
The argument from evil challenges the idea that perfect goodness is actually present in a being that also has complete knowledge and power, though this entry does not resolve that larger debate.

In a no-best-world situation, every world that could be chosen has a morally better alternative. Some philosophers think this makes perfect goodness impossible; others distinguish an outcome from the quality of the choice.

Freedom creates another puzzle. If being free means being able to choose wrongly, then necessary perfect goodness may seem incompatible with freedom. Other accounts of freedom reject that requirement.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic connects ideas about God with general questions about ethics and decision-making. It asks whether goodness lies mainly in outcomes, intentions, character, or responsiveness to reasons. It also reminds us that “perfect” does not always mean the same thing for every kind of being. These distinctions help explain why philosophers can agree that goodness matters while disagreeing about what perfect goodness requires.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical approach that describes God by asking what qualities an absolutely perfect being would need.
The highest possible excellence in a being’s choices, character, desires, and actions.
A quality that is excellent in itself, not merely because it suits a particular kind of creature.
A quality that is excellent for members of a particular kind but is not automatically better for every kind of being.
Whether something must be true, could be true, or happens only by accident or circumstance.
The power to choose and act without being controlled or forced by another cause.
The thought that what someone morally ought to do must be something that person is able to do.

questions_to_think_about: Should we judge a decision by its result, its reasons, or both?
Can someone be responsible for doing good if doing wrong is impossible for that person?
Is a quality that is excellent for humans automatically excellent for every possible being?
Would a perfectly good being have to create the best possible world?
